Surat al-'Adiyat is Meccan. [Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "It was revealed while al-'Adiyat was in Mecca." See: al-Durr al-Manthur, 8/599.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

* *

﴿By the charging steeds, panting,﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, Qatadah, the two Muqatils [meaning Muqatil ibn Hayyan and Muqatil ibn Sulayman], Abu al-'Aliyah, and others said: they are the galloping horses in the way of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that pant. Al-dabh (panting) is the sound of their insides when they run.

Ibn 'Abbas said: No animal pants except the horse, the dog and the fox. These animals pant only when their condition changes due to exhaustion or fright. The word is derived from the Arabic saying "dabahtuhu al-nar," meaning the fire changed its color.

[His words ﴿ḍabḥan﴾ are in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar); the implied meaning is: "and the chargers pant with panting."]

'Ali said: They are camels during the Hajj, running from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and from Muzdalifah to Mina. He also said that it was revealed concerning the Battle of Badr, [which was the first military campaign in Islam, Badr] and there were only two horses with us: a horse for al-Zubayr and a horse for al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. So how can the charging horses be meant? This view was also held by Ibn Mas'ud, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and al-Suddi.

Some who said they are camels stated: His words "ḍabḥan" mean "ḍibaḥan," stretching their necks while walking.

[Al-Tabari (30/271–273) related these opinions, which go back to two views, then gave preference, saying: "The more correct of the two views is the view of those who said that what is meant by al-'Adiyat is the horses, because camels do not pant; only horses pant, and Allah has informed that they run panting."]

﴿By those that strike sparks with their hooves﴾. Ikrimah, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: these are the horses, which strike fire with their hooves when they travel over stones. The meaning is: "by the horses that strike sparks with their hooves."

Qatadah said: these are the horses that stir up war and the fire of enmity between their riders.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: these are the horses that go out to fight in the cause of God, then return at night to their resting places, where they kindle their fire and prepare their food.

Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam said: these are the cunning of men, meaning the men of war. The Arabs say, when a man intends to deceive his companion: "By God, I will surely strike sparks for you, then I will surely kindle the fire for you."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: these are the fires that gather...[[al-Tabari (30/273–274) mentioned these opinions and then said, giving preference: "The most correct of these views is to say: God, may He be remembered, swore by the things that kindle fires by striking sparks. Horses kindle with their hooves, people kindle with flint, and the tongue, for example, kindles with speech, and men kindle with deceit, for example. Likewise, horses stir up war between their riders when they meet in battle. God has not indicated that the intended meaning is some of these rather than others. So everything that kindles fire by striking sparks is included in what He swore by, because of the general apparent meaning."]].

﴿By those that charge at dawn﴾. These are the horses that attack the enemy with their riders at the time of morning. This is the view of most commentators. Al-Qurazi said: these are the camels that carry their riders hurrying from Jam' [[Muzdalifah.]] to Mina on the Day of Sacrifice. The Sunnah is that they should not be pushed [with their riders on the Day of Sacrifice] [[The words between the brackets are omitted in "b".]] until morning. Al-Igharah (the raid) means hastening the journey. From this comes their saying: "Let Thabir see the sunrise, that we may raid."

﴿and raise dust thereby﴾, that is, they stir up [the ground] by the place of their travel [[In "b": "their travel".]]. This is a kinayah (an allusion) for something not mentioned, because the meaning is understood. ﴿a cloud of dust﴾ means dust, and naq' is dust.

﴿and penetrate thereby into the midst of the host﴾, that is, they enter with it into the middle of the enemy's host, which is the battalion. It is said: wasatu al-qawm (without doubling the sin), wassatuhum (with doubling), and tawassatuhum (with the reflexive form), all with one meaning. Al-Qurazi said: these are the camels that penetrate into the people [[The words between the brackets are omitted in "b".]], meaning the gathering at Mina. [This is the place of the oath.] [[The words between the brackets are omitted in "b".]] God swore by these things.

﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatādah said: "al-kanūd" means one who is disbelieving and who denies the blessings of Allah, exalted is He. Al-Kalbī said: In the dialect of Mudar and Rabīʿah, it means al-kafūr (the ungrateful), and in the dialect of Kindah and Ḥaḍramawt, it means al-ʿāṣī (the disobedient) [[See: Shuʿab al-Īmān by al-Bayhaqī: 8/507.]].

Al-Ḥasan said: It is the one who counts calamities and forgets blessings [[Narrated by al-Bayhaqī in "al-Shuʿab": 8/508, and al-Suyūṭī attributed it to Ibn Jarīr, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in "al-Shuʿab".]]. ʿAṭāʾ said: It is the one who does not give during a calamity that befalls his people.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: It is one who has little good. And "al-arḍ al-kanūd" is the land that produces nothing.

Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: "al-Kanūd" is one whom a single act of wrongdoing makes forget the many acts of kindness, and "al-Shakūr" is one whom a single act of kindness makes forget the many acts of wrongdoing.

﴿And indeed, he is a witness to that.﴾ [Most of the exegetes] [[In "B" (the second manuscript): the exegetes.]] said: And indeed, Allah is a witness to his being ungrateful. Ibn Kaysān said: The pronoun refers back to al-insān (man), meaning: he is a witness against himself by what he does.

﴿And indeed, he﴾, meaning man, ﴿is intensely attached to wealth﴾, meaning he loves wealth, ﴿and he is severe in it﴾, meaning he is stingy. That is, because of his love of wealth, he is stingy. It is said of the miser: "shadīd" (severe) and "mutashaddid" (rigid).

It was also said: The meaning is: "And indeed, he, in his love of wealth, is strong," that is, intense in his love of wealth.

﴿Does he not know﴾, meaning: Does this man not know, ﴿when what is in the graves is scattered﴾, meaning: is raised up and brought out, ﴿[from the dead]﴾ [[The words in brackets are omitted from "B".]].

﴿And what is in the breasts is brought out﴾, meaning: what is in them of good or evil is distinguished and made manifest.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 100, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, their Lord, about them,﴾ [gathered] [[In "b" it is "yajma'" (gathers).]] the pronoun, because al-Insan (mankind) is a noun of genus. ﴿On that Day, is All-Aware﴾, i.e., knowing. Al-Zajjaj said: Indeed Allah is All-Aware of them on that Day and on other than it, but the meaning is that He will recompense them for their disbelief on that [Day]. [[What is between the brackets is omitted from "b".]]
